# Hardware

`customer_support.offering.product.hardware` · offering_type · parent `customer_support.offering.product`

> A physical unit the customer owns, installs and operates, usually for years. Every fix has a shipping address. Nothing about a hardware resolution moves at software speed: the diagnosis is performed remotely through a human being who is standing next to the device and describing it badly, and the remedy is a part, a technician or a return — all of which travel at the speed of logistics and none of which we can perform ourselves at two in the morning. We can diagnose unilaterally and we can resolve almost nothing unilaterally, which is the exact inverse of software and the reason the two feel so different to run. Entitlement attaches to a serial number and a ship date rather than to a login, so the first question of a hardware ticket is one a hosted-software agent never asks: is this unit still covered, and can we prove when it left the factory. Failure is correlated by manufacturing lot rather than by release date, which means the cluster that matters looks nothing like a regression spike — it builds slowly over months as a fleet ages, and it is completely invisible unless serial numbers are on the tickets. The habit that breaks operators arriving from software is announcing a timeline on the strength of a diagnosis. "We have found the fix" is a meaningful sentence about a deploy and an empty one about a component that is not yet in a van, and the customer will quote the first date they were given back to us for the rest of the warranty.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | a physical unit shipped once, then owned and operated by the customer well beyond the point at which we still sell it |
| pricing_shape | one-off purchase carrying a warranty term, frequently plus a separately sold maintenance or support contract that is the real entitlement |
| margin_profile | moderate unit margin, and every dispatch, spare and return is a direct cash cost against it — support here consumes inventory and travel, not only labour |
| post_sale_load | a long obligation tail; the failure rate rises as the fleet ages, so the cheapest support year is the first one and nobody budgets for the fifth |
| support_load | bimodal — a heavy front band of installation and configuration questions in the first weeks after shipment, then a slow-burning fault stream that grows with fleet age. Batch defects produce spikes tied to manufacturing lots rather than to anything on our calendar, and they surface as a rising rate rather than as an outage |
| resolution_locus | a device in the customer's physical possession. The fix is a part, a field visit or an RMA, and the customer or a field engineer performs it — we hold the knowledge and none of the hands |
| notes | Firmware blurs this: a firmware defect has a software resolution locus and a hardware entitlement model, and a queue that treats it as one or the other will get the fix speed or the warranty question wrong. Flagging firmware tickets separately is worth the effort.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `external_ref`, `commitment_ref`


> `external_ref` carries the serial or RMA number and is not optional in this branch for two independent reasons: without unit identity the ticket cannot be clustered by manufacturing lot, which is the only clustering that pays for itself here, and a warranty claim cannot be proved when the customer disputes the ship date. `commitment_ref` is mandatory because a hardware promise is a date on which a physical object arrives — the customer is tracking that date whether or not we are.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `effective_at`, `expires_at`, `coverage_hours`


> Warranty starts at delivery, not at purchase, and the gap between those two dates is where most warranty disputes live. `effective_at` is therefore required here in a way it is not for a subscription, where the two are the same instant.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `verified_against_version`


> Hardware revisions ship under the same product name for years. An article written for revision B served confidently to the owner of a revision C unit produces a precise, authoritative instruction that damages an in-warranty device — a failure mode software support does not have, because software customers cannot physically break the thing by following our advice.
